## Before you start

Read a [short introduction](https://rspatial.org/spatial/index.html) to spatial data in R.  

There are a lot of questions. At first, do not spend too much time on making the perfect maps (you can come back to that later)

## Introduction

In this lab we will use some GPS tracking data for Blue Whales in the eastern North Pacific, downloaded from Movebank <https://www.movebank.org> which has lots of wildlife tracking data. We will make some maps and overlay polygons of Marine Protected Areas off the California coast to understand how whales move into and out of MPAs.

## Whale data

1. Use `terra::vect` to read in the datapoints for the Blue Whale migration data ("points.shp"). 

```{r blue}
library(terra)
bluew <- vect("~/Downloads/ESP_106/ESP 106/esp106_CandyGArellano/Week 6/Lab 6/Blue Whale Migration Data/points.shp")
bluew
```

This is a set of point location for GPS tagged blue whales the eastern north Pacific. Identifiers for individual whales are given in the ind_ident column. 

2) How many observations are there in this dataset? And how many individual whales are tracked? 

```{r nobs}
#get number of rows 
nrow(bluew)

#row names
names(bluew)   

#individual whales 
table(bluew$ind_ident)
length(unique(bluew$ind_ident))

# Answer: There are 15545 observations in the dataset, and 141 individual whales are tracked. 

```

## Mapping whales

3. Get the global country boundaries with the geodata package 

```{r wrld}
library(geodata)

```

```{r}
#checking working directory to make sure it's in Week 6 
getwd()

#path already set 
wrld <- geodata::world(path=".")
```


4. Make a plot showing the whale observations, using a different color for each whale (many colors will be alike). Add the west coast of North America for reference. Set the limits of the plot to the extent of the whale migration data. 

Refine the below. Plot 1 on canvas shows you what you can aim for.

```{r plotobs}
#checking crs
crs(bluew) #WGS 84 & EPSG 4326
crs(wrld)  #unknown CRS & two EPSG 

#because they're different, project wrld to match bluew CRS
wrld <- project(wrld, crs(bluew))

crs(wrld)

```

```{r}
# Step 1. plot the countries using the extent of the whale data to only show the area of interest. 
aoi <- ext(bluew) + 2.  ## area of interest

plot(wrld, ext=aoi, ##wrld will be plotted according to extent aoi 
     col ="grey90", #fill color
     border = "grey10") #border color 

#Step 2: plot the whale points. You can use either the "points" method or "plot( , add=TRUE)". The latter is easier for coloring, but you need to tell it not to add a legend.

whale_ids <- as.factor(bluew$ind_ident) #whale ID for each point 

color_palette <- hcl.colors(nlevels(whale_ids), "Dark 3") #section colors 

point_colors <- color_palette[as.integer(whale_ids)] #coloring each point by while type

plot(bluew,add=TRUE,
     col = point_colors, #color of each point
     pch = 16, #solid circles 
     cex = 0.5, #making the circles smaller 
     legend = FALSE) #adding whale points #no legend like in example

```


5) make new SpatVectors for each of the following two individuals: "2008CA-Bmu-00825" and "2005CA-Bmu-10821"

```{r spatv}
#subset from bluew SpatVector, identifiers for individual whales in ind_ident  

whale_08 <- bluew[bluew$ind_ident == "2008CA-Bmu-00825", ]

whale_05 <- bluew[bluew$ind_ident == "2005CA-Bmu-10821", ]

```



6) Combine these two into one new SpatVector 

```{r comb}

whales <- rbind(whale_08, whale_05)

#checking results 
whales
nrow(whales)
unique(whales$ind_ident)

```


7) Make a map showing the tracks of these two using different colors. See plot2 on Canvas for an example.

```{r tracks}
##wrld is greater SpatVector w country polygons. ext() used as boundary

aoi_2 <- ext(whales) # area of interest for this plot 

plot(wrld, ext=aoi_2, 
     col = "grey80", border = "grey0")

plot(whale_05, add = TRUE, 
     col = "red", 
     pch = 16, 
     cex = 0.4)

plot(whale_08, add = TRUE, 
     col = "blue", 
     pch = 16, 
     cex = 0.4)
```

## Protected areas

8) The folder MPAs has a shapefile with polygons for Marine Protected Areas within the United States. This file was extracted from a file with all protected areas in the US [source](https://www.protectedplanet.net). Read the MPA shapefile. 

```{r PAs}
mpa <- vect("~/Downloads/ESP_106/ESP 106/esp106_CandyGArellano/Week 6/Lab 6/MPAs/mpas.shp")
```

9) Now we will focus on just the US west coast. You can use the following longitude and latitude extent: xmin=-128, xmax=-115, ymin=32, ymax=40. Get just the MPAs on the US west coast by cropping the MPA dataset to this extent.

```{r ext}
#Hint: use the crop() function
##basically defining a bounding box
?crop #can crop via rows and columns 

#defining extent 
west_ext <- ext(-128, -115, 32, 40)

#fitting mpa to given extent
mpa <- crop(mpa, west_ext)
```

10) Find the fraction of the blue whale observations that are in one of the west coast MPAs. You can use `is.related`

```{r frac}
?is.related #is.related(x,y,relation)

#finding points that intersect with polygon, will be boolean 
inside_obs <- is.related(bluew, mpa, relation = "intersects")

#how many true values are inside 
sum(inside_obs)

#computing fraction
fraction_inside <- sum(inside_obs)/nrow(bluew)

fraction_inside 

```

11) Find what fraction of blue whales in the dataset spend at least some time in one of these west coast MPAs. 

```{r fracMPA}

inside_pts <- bluew[inside_obs, ] #keeping TRUE values within inside_obs boolean collection

whales_inside_mpa <- unique(inside_pts$ind_ident) #finding whales that appear inside MPA 

total_whales <- unique(bluew$ind_ident) #total whales 

fraction_whales <- length(whales_inside_mpa) / length(total_whales) #taking fraction 

fraction_whales

```


12. Create a raster with counts of blue whale observations along the California coast. Use the spatial extent we used for the mpa data (question 8) and use a spatial resolution of 1/6th of a degree. First create an empty SpatRaster. Then use `rasterize`

```{r rcount}
#note extent is already defined as aoi. 
?rasterize #note that "count" needs replacement

#raster 
r <- rast(ext = aoi, res=1/6, crs = crs(bluew))

#how many observations along Coast
counts <- rasterize(bluew, r, fun="length")

#results
counts

plot(counts, main = "Blue whale observations") #it rasterized, yay


```

13. Make a map to show the counts and the MPAs and land areas. Plot 3 on Canvas shows you the plot you are aiming for. 

```{r countmap}
#making sure land geography is cropped to raster extent
geo <- crop(wrld, ext(counts))

#plotting counts raster 
plot(counts, main = "Blue Whale Observations in MPAs") 

#adding land geography  
plot(geo, add = TRUE, 
     col = "grey90", 
     border = "grey40")

#adding MPA's in red 
plot(mpa, add = TRUE, 
     col = NA, 
     border = "red", 
     lwd = 1)


```

14) Using a subset of the country boundaries (to speed up computations), create a raster with the distance to the coast, using the raster with the number of observations as template.

```{r distcoast}
coast <- crop(wrld, ext(counts)+1)

#turning polygons into raster 
LandGeo_Raster <- rasterize(coast, counts, field = 1)

#distance to nearest land
dist_coast <- distance(LandGeo_Raster)

```

15) For each blue whale observation, find the distance to the coast based on this raster (you can use `terra::extract`). Make a histogram of the distribution. 

```{r extract}
#get distance values
d15 <- terra::extract(dist_coast, bluew)

distance_values <- d15[[2]]

#histogram
hist(distance_values, 
     breaks = 30,
     main = "Blue whale observations: distance to coast",
     xlab = "Distance to coast in meters")


```
